title: FreeRTOS simulation layer and test framework
summary: A host-side FreeRTOS simulation layer that lets production firmware written for an ESP32 build and run as an ordinary Linux program. It made unit tests, sanitizers and coverage possible in CI. The shim and the test migration took about four weeks, and I did it on my own.
highlights: Re-implements the FreeRTOS API surface the firmware calls (tasks, delays, ticks, timers, concurrency primitives), so unmodified application code links against it on x86.
Time is a global tick counter that tests advance programmatically: a test says "advance 50 ticks" and every vTaskDelay returns deterministically.
Interrupt-driven paths were left out on purpose. Simulating ISRs is its own problem and the first modules did not need it.
The earlier dual-chip firmware's unit tests were ported to the single-MCU architecture by updating paths, syntax, mocks and flags, after proving the approach on a few simple layers first.
AddressSanitizer, UBSan and Valgrind found real memory leaks and invalid writes in code that had run on hardware undetected, and coverage rose from 45% to 80%.

details.label: Problem
details.body: The company's current device runs FreeRTOS on a single MCU, and much of the production firmware (HAL utilities, a debouncer, time-dependent logic) calls FreeRTOS directly: vTaskDelay, tick counts, software timers. A normal Linux process has none of that, so every test run needed a physical ESP32. That is slow, hard to run in CI, and rules out sanitizers, which are host tools that cannot run on the embedded target.

details.label: Reusing instead of rewriting
details.body: My first task was a unit test suite for the single-MCU architecture. Rather than write tests from scratch I studied the earlier dual-chip architecture the company had moved on from, which already had tests, and saw that the underlying layers shared the same code skeletons. I proved the idea on a few simple layers, then scaled it across the modules by updating include paths, syntax, mocks and build flags. The test framework moved from Ceedling 0.31 to 1.x along the way, and CI runs in Docker on GitHub Actions.

details.label: The shim
details.body: Many of those modules still called FreeRTOS, so I wrote a C/C++ layer exposing the same API as the real one but implemented for the host. The tick counter is a global that tests advance, so time becomes an input rather than something the machine decides. Delays and timers hang off the same counter. The result is that source files that used to be locked to the hardware compile and run under Ceedling and Unity on a CI runner with deterministic time.

details.label: What it caught
details.body: Once the code ran on the host I added AddressSanitizer, UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer and Valgrind to the test runs. They found real memory leaks, over-initialized buffers and invalid or overflowing writes in code derived from the older firmware, which had been running on hardware without anyone noticing. Code coverage tooling went into the same pipeline, and coverage rose from 45% to 80%. Failures that used to surface late on a device now surface on a laptop, before hardware testing starts.

details.label: Scope
details.body: I deliberately did not simulate interrupt service routines. The shim covers the modules that needed coverage first, and the code stays at the company, so this page describes the design.
